evidence: Plaut. Cist. 1.1.120: aurēs graviter obtundō tuās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally “beat against, blunt”: to tire someone by saying a thing too often or too long. “You’re boring me” is obtundis (Ter. And. 348, see understand).

evidence: Traupman 94: nē sīs odiōsus, “don’t be a bore”
terms.comment: Of a person or a thing that gets on one’s nerves; odiōsus esse is “to be a bore”.
Troublesome, a nuisance; nisi molestum est, “if it’s no trouble”.

phrases.latin: aurēs graviter obtundō tuās, nē quem amēs
phrases.english: I keep dinning it into your ears that you shouldn’t fall in love with anyone

sources: Lewis & Short: obtundo · Lewis & Short: odiosus · Lewis & Short: molestus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 94, 281.
Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them and have not been checked against an edition.
